content: The first three policies focus on various aspects of the education sector and the dynamics of the health labor market. These policies are interconnected within a system that follows an input-throughput-output sequence. Policies regulating the private sector encompass the entire scope of the health labor market. 1. Health Labor Market Framework: This framework begins with high school education in health, leading to a pool of qualified health workers. These workers may enter the healthcare sector, other sectors, or remain unemployed or out of the labor force. Some may pursue education in other fields or work abroad. The ultimate goal is to achieve universal health coverage (UHC) with safe, effective, and person-centered health services. Production Policies: These include policies on infrastructure, materials, student enrollment, student selection, and teaching staff. Policies on Inflows and Outflows: These address migration, emigration, attracting unemployed health workers, and reintegrating health workers into the healthcare sector. Policies on Maldistribution and Inefficiencies: These aim to improve productivity, performance, skill mix composition, and retention of health workers in underserved areas. Private Sector Regulation Policies: These focus on managing dual practice, improving training quality, and enhancing service delivery. 2. National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA): The NHWA framework includes 10 modules with 78 core indicators designed to support national health workforce (HWF) policies, advancing progress toward UHC and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). These indicators address three key labor market components: education, labor force, and population health needs. Module 1: Active Health Workforce Stock: This module provides a detailed overview of the composition and distribution of the health workforce (HWF) by geography, age, sex, institutional sector, and facility type. It identifies gaps in professions, competencies, and geographic or sectoral distribution, enabling targeted policy interventions. Modules 2, 3, and 4: Education: These modules support the sustainable expansion and reform of HWF education and training to increase the quantity, quality, and relevance of the workforce. They guide efforts to align the workforce with health promotion, disease prevention, primary care, and community-based services. 3. Health Labor Market Dynamics: Module 5: Health Labor Market Flows: This module tracks entries and exits from the labor market, differentiating between domestic efforts and reliance on foreign health workers. It also monitors vacancies and unemployment to inform recruitment and retention policies. Module 6: Employment Characteristics and Working Conditions: This module examines employment conditions, working hours, and labor market dynamics, contributing to the promotion of decent work and work-life balance. Module 7: Health Workforce Spending and Remuneration: This module maps expenditures on the health workforce, including private sector earnings, supporting SDG goals on decent work and gender equality. 4. Skill Mix and Governance: Module 8: Skill Mix Composition for Models of Care: This module analyzes the skill mix of the workforce to align labor supply with healthcare needs, emphasizing primary care and patient-centered care. Module 9: Governance and Health Workforce Policies: This module evaluates governance mechanisms, intersectoral coordination, and alignment of education plans with national health plans. Module 10: Health Workforce Information Systems (HRHIS): This module assesses the readiness of HRHIS to meet international reporting requirements and track workforce outputs, labor market entrants, and facility locations. 5. Implementation of NHWA: The NHWA is a country-led initiative that builds on national systems and existing mechanisms for data collection and evaluation of the health workforce. WHO provides tools, including a handbook, implementation guide, and web platform for data reporting and visualization. The NHWA supports policy-making by offering both numeric and capability indicators, enabling countries to address health workforce priorities effectively. 6. Financial indicators are standardized to USD for international comparisons, and population estimates are aligned with global standards. 7. Occupational Classifications and Social Workers: NHWA indicators are based on internationally agreed occupational classifications, such as ISCO-08. While the focus is on health workers, countries are encouraged to track data on social workers employed in health facilities for a broader understanding of health-related activities. 8. Deviations from Definitions: Member States are encouraged to report data even if they deviate from NHWA definitions, provided the methodology used is clearly described.
